rappel_detail.notes: Rappel 1 of 4 on a single 60 m rope: a short rappel from the summit bolts down the uppermost pitch to the two-bolt station at the top of pitch 3.
hazards: A crack a couple of feet below the summit bolts is notorious for wedging rope. Stopping at the pitch-3 ledge instead of running the rope through to the top of pitch 2 is the accepted way to avoid it, and is the single most repeated warning on this descent.
Serpentine is slick rock, and slicker still when damp or dusty; the summit stance is small and the start of the rappel is over the edge rather than off a ledge.
rappel_detail.station: The three-bolt anchor on the serpentine summit block at the top of the climb. The rappel off it is short and awkward — a sit-and-spin start straight off the bolts — and drops the last pitch to a two-bolt station on a narrow ledge at the top of pitch 3. Break here even though the terrain below looks like it would go in one longer rappel.

rappel_detail.anchor: two bolts on a narrow ledge, top of pitch 3
hazards: Coming up short leaves the rappeller hanging on a slick serpentine face above the ledge. Knot the ends and confirm the rope reaches before the last person commits.

A crack near the second slung boulder at the end of pitch 2 has wedged a rope end on the pull; the pitch is easy enough that one party simply scrambled back up to free it, but that is luck rather than a plan.
rappel_detail.station: Two bolts on a narrow ledge at the top of pitch 3, replacing older pitons. The rappel aims for the large ledge with a slung boulder near the top of pitch 2. A 60 m rope comes up about 5 m (15 ft) short of that ledge and a 70 m only just makes it, so on a 60 m finish with a short downclimb on Class 3 rock to the ledge.

wa_east_ridge_9.rappels: Do not rappel the East Ridge. Descend the South Ridge line from the three-bolt summit anchor: 4 rappels on a single 60 m rope, one per pitch, or three on two 60 m ropes.
wa_east_ridge_9.rappel_count_note: The East Ridge has no good rappel anchors, so the descent is the South Ridge rappel line. Counted for one 60 m rope: one rappel per pitch, summit to the pitch-3 bolts, pitch 3 to the big ledge above pitch 2 (the rope comes up about 15 ft short, so downclimb the last bit), pitch 2 to the top of pitch 1, and pitch 1 to the base. With two 60 m ropes it is three: the same first two, then one long rappel from the pitch-2 ledge to the base. On any setup, do not run one long rappel from the summit to the top of pitch 2: a crack just under the summit bolts and another near the slung boulder at the end of pitch 2 are both known rope-eaters.
wa_east_ridge_9.descent_text: Do not rappel the East Ridge itself: the ridgeline lacks good rappel anchors and is loose and exposed in a way that makes retracing it dangerous. Instead, from the summit, scramble back to the North-South ridge crest and use the South Ridge rappel line from its three-bolt summit anchor. On a single 60 m rope it is four rappels, one per pitch: a short one to the two-bolt station at the top of pitch 3; one toward the big ledge with a slung boulder above pitch 2, which comes up about 15 ft short so you downclimb the last bit; one down pitch 2 to the top of pitch 1; and one to the base. With two 60 m ropes it is three, going straight from the pitch-2 ledge to the base. Do not skip from the summit straight to the top of pitch 2 in one long rappel: a crack just below the top anchor is known for jamming ropes. Anchors are a mix of fixed bolts and natural slung-boulder anchors reinforced with webbing, so carry spare tat. From the base, downclimb the class 3-4 gully back to the notch and retrace the approach across the slabs to Lake Ingalls and out via Ingalls Pass to the trailhead.

wa_ingalls_peak_south_ridge.rappels: 4 rappels on a single 60 m rope from the three-bolt summit anchor, with a short downclimb to the pitch-2 ledge where the rope comes up short. Two 60 m ropes cut it to three.
wa_ingalls_peak_south_ridge.rappel_count_note: Counted for one 60 m rope: summit to the pitch-3 bolts, pitch 3 to the big ledge above pitch 2 (the rope comes up about 15 ft short, so downclimb the last bit), pitch 2 to the top of pitch 1, and pitch 1 to the base. With two 60 m ropes it is three: the same first two, then one long rappel from the pitch-2 ledge to the base. On any setup, do not run one long rappel from the summit to the top of pitch 2: a crack just under the summit bolts and another near the slung boulder at the end of pitch 2 are both known rope-eaters.
wa_ingalls_peak_south_ridge.descent_text: Descend by rappelling the South Ridge climbing line itself (or, for parties who diverge, the closely parallel Southwest Face). From the summit it is four rappels on a single 60 m rope, or three with two 60 m ropes, described here for two ropes: (1) a single-strand rappel down the uppermost pitch to a two-bolt anchor on a narrow ledge; (2) a full-length rappel (double-rope length, i.e. using the rope doubled) down to a large ledge/slung boulder near the top of pitch 2 - do not be tempted to skip straight from the summit to the top of pitch 2 in one long rappel, since a crack just below the top anchor is notorious for wedging and stuck ropes have resulted; breaking it at the pitch-3 ledge avoids this; and (3) a final rappel from that ledge down to the base ledges/gully where the climb started. Anchors are a mix of fixed two-bolt stations and natural slung-boulder/horn anchors reinforced with webbing - carry a few extra feet of tat/webbing since the natural anchors get replaced periodically and can be tired. Below the last rappel, downclimb the class 3-4 gully back to the notch and retrace the approach talus/slabs to Lake Ingalls and out via Ingalls Pass.

wa_garfield_mountain_southwest_ledges.rappels: Counts for this rappel line differ - about 20 to 25 double-rope rappels down the Infinite Bliss line off its chain stations, with two 60 m ropes, interspersed with downclimbing. A 70 m or 80 m single rope is not long enough for those stations.
wa_garfield_mountain_southwest_ledges.descent_text: From the summit block reverse the heather benches and downclimb back into the Infinite Bliss line, then rappel the entire route — roughly 20 double-rope rappels off the chain stations with two 60 m ropes, interspersed with downclimbing. A 70 m or 80 m single rope is NOT long enough for the Infinite Bliss stations. Watch for parties climbing below you; the whole descent runs down a gully-slab that funnels anything you dislodge straight onto them. Budget 3-4 hours minimum for the rappels and start them with enough daylight left — a 2014 fatality on this rappel line happened when a climber skipped a station in fading light and rappelled off unknotted rope ends.

wa_promised_land.rappels: Rappel by way of Sisyphus, or scramble to the top. Rappelling from below the treed ledge takes two 60 m ropes.

wa_south_rib.rappels: Rappelling the rib itself needs double ropes and much downclimbing and is not recommended. The standard exit traverses north over the subsummits to one rappel of about 30 m from a slung tree at the middle summit, then the Southeast Couloir.

wa_half_moon_southwest_slopes.rappels: The route is descended by rappelling the line of ascent back to the notch. Carry two ropes. Anchors are a mix of fixed pitons, bolts, slung horns and nuts of varying age, and some parties have found none at all, so bring slings and cord to back up or build each station.
wa_half_moon_southwest_slopes.descent_text: Descend the route. From the summit, downclimb the easy but exposed top of the ridge to the first anchor and rappel back down the line of ascent, using the ledges on the crest and its west side as stations, until you are back in the notch north of the peak. Carry two ropes; the stations are a mix of old fixed pitons, bolts, slung horns and nuts, some parties have found no fixed anchors at all, and any tat left there should be inspected and backed up. From the notch, descend the loose scree gully carefully (keep the party close to limit rockfall), and at its foot rejoin the climbers' path and follow it back north to the hairpin pullout on the highway. In mid-September the top pitch was descended on a single-rope rappel, and from the lower ledges a hidden anchor (a nut plus a horn) lies a scramble away, first climber's left then right; the last rappel from the first-pitch ledge drops straight to the ground with no need to traverse.
